metadata.title: Claude, Escalation Flagger.
metadata.purpose: Answer whether a Claude Skill named escalation-flagger flags things by Claude's own judgment about what looks risky, or by a match against criteria written down in a file -- using the general mechanism every Claude Skill shares (a folder, one SKILL.md, criteria checked in order) since the source never states escalation-flagger's specific criteria or escalation target. Lands the carry-out that a flag is a match against a written file, not a judgment call: reliable inside what's written, silent past its edge.
metadata.anchor_pair: B01 -> B03 (the SKILL.md card with its numbered checklist of criteria, run twice with identical match-and-flag results, then a case outside the file with nothing to match)

beats.narration_text: People assume it decides what's risky. Look at the mechanism — it doesn't decide. It reads a file, checks a list, matches. The honest question isn't what it thinks — it's what it matches.

beats.narration_text: Here's what a Claude Skill actually is: a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one, escalation-flagger, keeps everything in one file — SKILL.md, plain sentences, not code. Open it: a numbered checklist of criteria, checked top to bottom. Anthropic optimized for auditability over cleverness. The file decides what gets flagged. Claude just runs the check.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — a SKILL.md card opening, a numbered checklist of criteria

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — SKILL.md, a numbered checklist
production_viz.mechanic: A folder labeled escalation-flagger opens into a SKILL.md card. A numbered checklist of criteria types itself in top to bottom, one lighting up with a checkmark. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The guess most people make: Claude senses which things feel risky. Falsify it. Delete a criterion from the file — inputs that used to trigger it stop being flagged. Nothing hidden fills the gap. The mechanism is a linear pass down a written list, flagging where one item matches. They chose transparency. The trade-off: anything the list doesn't name is invisible.

shot.new_visual_element: The wrong guess, drawn then struck; the checklist mechanism

production_viz.label: Checked, not sensed
production_viz.mechanic: An input checked against a linear list of criteria, one item at a time; one criterion struck out in crimson; the same input then passes through afterward with no flag.

beats.narration_text: Back to that same SKILL.md. Run the same input through twice — you get the same match, the same flag, every time. That's not intelligence; it's determinism. Now send a case the list never anticipated. Nothing gets flagged — not because Claude judged it safe, but because nothing in the file matched it. Reliable inside what's written. Silent past its edge.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same SKILL.md card, run twice, then a case with nothing to match

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same match, then no match
production_viz.mechanic: THE B01 COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical — the same SKILL.md card, run twice side by side, the same criterion lit both times. Then a new input shape passes down the list with no matching criterion and exits unflagged.

beats.narration_text: A flag isn't Claude's judgment — it's a match against text in a file. Same match, same flag, every time. No match, no flag, however it looks to a person.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Ask it to draft a SKILL.md for a real escalation-flagger — three numbered match rules, then two test inputs, one that matches and one that doesn't. Watch the flag follow the file, not a feeling. Go deeper: delete one rule, and see which inputs stop being flagged — and what that reveals about what your list actually covers.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to see the mechanism of a Claude Skill's escalation-flagger in action. Draft a SKILL.md for one escalation criterion I'd want in a real workflow — pick a domain (customer support, code review, or medical intake) — and write it as a numbered checklist of three concrete match rules a Claude agent could evaluate against any input. Then run two test inputs through it: one that matches a specific rule (name which) and one that doesn't. For each, show exactly what the flag output would look like.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: delete one of the three rules. Which inputs stop being flagged, and what does that reveal about what your list actually covers versus what you assumed it did?
